opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me, it's a real pleasure to be here.

What I find most interesting is that people trained in mathematics share a certain instinct. You spend years staring at a problem you can't solve, and you learn to live with that discomfort. You learn that a proof is either correct or it isn't, and there's no partial credit from the universe. So when mathematicians start thinking about AI, they bring a very particular kind of honesty. They ask, "Okay, but does the model actually *know* this, or is it pattern-matching its way to something that looks right?"

That question turns out to be central right now. A lot of the excitement around AI comes from fluency: models that write beautifully and sound confident. Mathematicians are naturally suspicious of fluency. In our world, a beautifully written wrong proof is still wrong. So conversations with them quickly get to the heart of things: how do we verify reasoning, how do we build systems where correctness can be checked rather than just asserted?

There's also a shared sense of taste. Good mathematicians have a feel for which problems are worth working on, which definitions are "right," and when a structure is hiding underneath a mess of special cases. Talking with people who have that taste and also understand how these models are trained gives you a different kind of conversation. It's not just "how do we scale this," but "what is the right abstraction here? What would it even mean for a machine to understand a concept?"

And personally, it feels a bit like finding people who speak the same native language. You can skip a lot of explanation. You can say "this feels like a compactness argument" or "this is a local-to-global problem," and they immediately get the intuition. That shorthand makes it possible to go much deeper, much faster. For me, a lot of my most exciting ideas have come out of exactly those conversations.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared mathematical instincts and says that combining mathematical taste with AI knowledge makes for a different, deeper conversation. It does not clearly identify new understandings that participants bring as the source of interest.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find most interesting is that people trained in mathematics tend to carry a very particular kind of honesty into their thinking about AI. When you've spent years sitting with a proof that won't close, you develop a feel for the difference between "this seems right" and "this is actually established." And I think that distinction is exactly what the AI conversation needs right now, because so much of the public discussion runs on vibes, on demos, on extrapolating from a few impressive examples.

So when I talk with other mathematicians who've gotten into AI, the conversation usually goes somewhere different. We're less interested in whether a model can produce something that looks like a solution and more interested in what it actually understands, whether there's structure underneath, whether the reasoning would survive a change in the problem. Mathematicians are naturally suspicious of answers that are correct for the wrong reasons, because we've all had that experience of a "proof" that worked by accident.

The other thing is that mathematics gives you a shared language for talking about limits. Not limits in the sense of "AI will never do X," but limits in the sense of understanding what a system is and isn't doing, what the objective really is, where the gaps are. I find those conversations much more generative than the ones that are purely optimistic or purely dismissive. People who've done serious math tend to hold both the excitement and the skepticism at the same time, and they can move between them without getting defensive.

And honestly, there's also something personal in it. A lot of us came to math because we loved the feeling of understanding something deeply and completely. AI is forcing us to ask what that feeling is really made of, whether it can be replicated, whether it should be. Those are questions I never expected to be asking when I started, and I think the people best equipped to think about them carefully are the ones who've felt that kind of understanding firsthand.

r001.rationale: The response says math-trained people bring a proof-based sense of rigor, a shared language for discussing AI’s limits, and a way to hold excitement and skepticism together, making their conversations different and more generative.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s interesting is that we have a shared language, but we don’t necessarily have the same intuitions. In mathematics, you’re often asking, “What are the assumptions? What can we prove?” With AI, you also have to ask, “What do we observe, and why does it work?” There’s a gap between those kinds of understanding, and I find that gap really fascinating.

So I enjoy hearing where someone’s mathematical intuition helps them think about AI—and where AI has surprised them enough that they’ve had to rethink that intuition. Those are often the conversations where I learn the most.

r001.rationale: The response says these conversations are interesting because people’s mathematical intuitions help them think about AI, while AI can surprise them and prompt new thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s interesting is that you have a shared language, but you don’t necessarily have the same intuitions. In mathematics, you’re often asking, “What are the assumptions? Can we make this precise? Can we prove it?” With AI, you also have to ask, “What happens when we actually run the experiment?” And those two ways of thinking can push against each other in a productive way.

So I enjoy hearing where someone’s mathematical intuition helps them understand AI, and where the behavior of AI has surprised them. Those surprises are often where the conversation gets really interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says it enjoys hearing how someone’s mathematical intuition helps them understand AI and what has surprised them, identifying participants’ perspectives and discoveries as a source of interest.
